overview.text: Hedda Gabler is a four-act play by Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen, published in 1890 and first performed in 1891. It is known as a psychological drama: rather than focusing only on outward events, it closely examines Hedda’s discontent and her attempts to influence the people around her. Newly married to Jørgen Tesman, Hedda becomes entangled in the fate of writer Eilert Løvborg and his manuscript. She secretly burns it, and later Judge Brack uses what he knows about a pistol to threaten her. As Tesman and Thea work to recreate the manuscript, Hedda sees her control slipping away and dies by suicide. The play’s tense relationships and focus on a complex central character distinguish it.

key_facts.text: The play has four acts; it was published in 1890 and first performed in 1891.
Hedda is General Gabler’s daughter and is newly married to Jørgen Tesman when the play begins.
Hedda burns Eilert Løvborg’s manuscript, which he had written with help from Thea Elvsted.
Judge Brack learns that Løvborg’s pistol belonged to Hedda’s father and plans to use this knowledge against her.
The play is described by Store norske leksikon as a psychological drama and a study of Hedda’s struggle to find meaning in life.
